# 10 - Legacy, Niche, and Non-Traction Chemistries

Acquisition method: Web research note synthesized from public sources.

Primary sources:

- NHTSA, Electric and Hybrid Vehicles: Battery, Charging & Safety: https://www.nhtsa.gov/vehicle-safety/electric-and-hybrid-vehicles
- DOE, DOE Explains Batteries: https://www.energy.gov/science/doe-explainsbatteries
- Battery University, summary table of lithium-based batteries: https://batteryuniversity.com/article/bu-216-summary-table-of-lithium-based-batteries
- IEA, Global EV Outlook 2025, advanced battery technologies: https://www.iea.org/reports/global-ev-outlook-2025/electric-vehicle-batteries

## Purpose

This file captures battery types that are relevant to mobility context but are unlikely to become mainstream passenger BEV traction batteries in the near future.

## LMO - Lithium Manganese Oxide

LMO uses a manganese spinel cathode. It can deliver high power and has been used historically in some EV and hybrid applications, often blended with other chemistries. Its lower energy density and aging limitations have reduced its role as a standalone modern BEV chemistry.

Relevance: historical and niche. It matters for understanding older EV packs and manganese-based development lineage.

## LTO - Lithium Titanate

LTO replaces graphite with lithium titanate at the anode. It offers excellent cycle life, safety, low-temperature operation, and fast charging, but has low energy density and higher cost.

Relevance: buses, industrial vehicles, fast-charge duty cycles, stationary storage, and extreme-cycle applications. Less suitable for mainstream passenger cars because range per kg and per liter is weak.

## NiMH - Nickel Metal Hydride

NiMH is important in hybrids and older electrified vehicles. It is durable and proven, but lower energy density and memory/cost characteristics make it uncompetitive for modern long-range BEVs.

Relevance: hybrids and historical context, not future mainstream BEV traction.

## Lead-Acid

Lead-acid remains common for 12 V auxiliary systems and low-voltage vehicle functions. It is cheap and recyclable but far too heavy and low-energy for modern traction packs.

Relevance: auxiliary batteries, not BEV propulsion.

## Metal-Air

Metal-air batteries, including lithium-air, zinc-air, and aluminum-air concepts, offer high theoretical energy density. Practical rechargeability, power, cycle life, air management, and system complexity remain major barriers.

Relevance: future research and specialty range-extension concepts, not credible near-term mainstream EV packs.

## Redox-Flow and Iron-Air

IEA lists redox-flow and iron-air among advanced batteries, but these target long-duration stationary storage more than cars. Their systems rely on tanks, pumps, or very low power-density architectures that do not fit passenger EV traction needs.

Relevance: grid storage and energy system context. They matter indirectly because cheaper grid storage can improve charging infrastructure and renewable electricity, but they are not car traction battery candidates.

## Practical Conclusion

For the electric car project, these chemistries should be treated as boundary-setting context. The main vehicle-value analysis should focus on LFP/LMFP, NMC/NCA/NMCA, LMR, sodium-ion, silicon-enhanced lithium-ion, semi-solid, all-solid-state, lithium-metal, and lithium-sulfur.
